title: The Well of Vessel Farm
premise: Oscar Vasquez takes a teaching post at Vessel Farm's village school, where a handful of pupils vanish each autumn and the parish records have been rewritten so thoroughly that no one remembers them. When the church bell—melted down in 1911—rings at midnight, Oscar discovers the village survives by feeding a chosen family to the well beneath the schoolhouse, and his own students are next on the count. Refusing the bargain that has kept everyone else alive, he smuggles the Aldridge children out while the villagers, led by the schoolmistress Mrs. Halloway, hunt them through the fog. In the end Oscar seals himself in the well in the children's place, breaking the cycle but not surviving it—and the bell rings once more, this time for him.
about_author: S. M. Sterling is the pen name of a former rural schoolteacher who spent nine years in villages small enough to keep their own records and their own silences. Their fiction draws on folk horror traditions and on the quiet cruelties communities commit to preserve themselves.

chapters.title: The Register
chapters.summary: POV: Oscar. Arriving at Vessel Farm, Oscar notices the school register skips certain names each October, as if pages were razored out. The headmistress, Mrs. Halloway, is warm but evasive; the children flinch when he mentions the well behind the playground. Emotional beat: unease disguised as professional optimism—he tells himself it's just a poor, insular place.

chapters.title: Attendance
chapters.summary: POV: Oscar. A boy named Tam Aldridge stops attending; his desk is removed overnight and no one will say where he went. Oscar walks to the Aldridge farm and finds the family frightened, compliant, and counting days on a chalkboard. Emotional beat: first real dread—the machinery of disappearance is domestic, ordinary, and agreed upon.

chapters.title: What the Bell Was
chapters.summary: POV: Oscar, with an interlude from elderly villager Edith Crane. Edith describes the 1911 melting of the church bell and the founding of 'the count.' That night Oscar hears a bell toll across empty fields. Emotional beat: the past asserting itself—the horror is not supernatural intrusion but a debt still being paid.

chapters.title: The Count
chapters.summary: POV: Oscar. He finds the ledger in the school cellar: every seven years one family is given to the well, and the village prospers—crops, health, silence. This year the mark falls on the Aldridges. Mrs. Halloway catches him reading and offers gentle, reasonable arguments. Emotional beat: temptation; survival dressed up as justice.

chapters.title: Halloway's Lesson
chapters.summary: POV: Mrs. Halloway. She recounts her own family's turn in the count two generations back and how she was spared by obedience. She warns Oscar that outsiders who interfere become part of the arithmetic. Emotional beat: chilling sympathy—the antagonist believes she is the moral one.

chapters.title: Fog Over the Fields
chapters.summary: POV: Oscar. With three nights until the count, Oscar plans the Aldridges' escape: the bus route is watched, the roads remembered. He recruits Edith, who gives him her late husband's truck and her guilt. Emotional beat: resolve hardening into conspiracy; he crosses from observer to accomplice.

chapters.title: The First Night of the Hunt
chapters.summary: POV: alternating Oscar and Tam Aldridge. The escape fails halfway—lanterns rise along the hedgerows, neighbors' faces familiar and blank. The Aldridge parents surrender themselves to buy the children time. Emotional beat: terror and heartbreak; the price of survival made flesh.

chapters.title: Beneath the Schoolhouse
chapters.summary: POV: Oscar. Descending into the well to hide the children, Oscar finds the previous families—not bones but presences, still waiting, still counted. The bell rings overhead, closer now, though there is no bell. Emotional beat: confrontation with what the village has actually been feeding all along.

chapters.title: The Reckoning Bell
chapters.summary: POV: Oscar and Mrs. Halloway. At the wellhead, Halloway demands the children; Oscar offers himself instead, arguing the well takes willingness, not innocence. The bell tolls thirteen times and the village's prosperity visibly begins to rot—blight creeping up the walls. Emotional beat: climax; justice outside any law, paid in person.

chapters.title: Roll Call
chapters.summary: POV: Tam Aldridge, epilogue. The children reach the city; the register at their new school lists them, present, whole. Back at Vessel Farm the school stands empty, the ledger closed, and on the last page a new name is written in fresh ink. Emotional beat: grief braided with peace—the debt transferred, the story sealed.
